title: Sort and Compare
context: Grade 3, the second working topic of the fractions chapter. An adult sees fractions being circled in a list, which a pencil does well. What is being settled is that the kind of a fraction is read from its two numbers: one on top, the top smaller than the bottom, or the bottoms matching. A child who watches only the size of the numbers will call 9/10 improper because nine and ten are big, or will call two fractions like because their top numbers match. A real pizza, bar or jug beside each card is what lets the child check a reading against something they can picture eating or pouring.

writeup.why: Read the kind of a fraction from its two numbers, tell like from unlike by the bottom numbers, and say which of two like fractions is bigger by comparing the top numbers, with a real pizza, bar or jug beside every card to check the reading.
writeup.look: A tray of fraction cards at the left, each beside a real object cut or filled to show it, two labelled bins at the right, a mat for two cards, and on the last phase two identical objects from one edge and a line-up row.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Sort and Compare' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many cards have been sorted so far, out of the cards on the tray. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The tray of cards stands at the left, its top left at x 80, y 230, six cards in three columns and two rows, each 190 by 150 with 15 between them. A card holds the fraction written large at its left, the top number above a level line above the bottom number, and its real object at its right, 120 across and 100 tall, drawn in natural colours: a pizza cut into slices, a chocolate bar with its squares, a jug of juice with equal marks, a plate of laddoos, a row of kites or a round cake. The parts the top number counts sit on a small deep blue plate under the object, labelled Taken, or inside a deep blue ring on a jug, and the parts left stay on the object. An improper card slides a second pizza, bar or cake in beside the first, so one whole and more is drawn, and a card with the same number top and bottom shows exactly one whole object inside a green outline labelled Whole. The two bins stand at the right of the working area, each 200 by 300 with its label on top, at x 700, y 230 and x 920, y 230 on the first two phases. On the third phase the bins give way to the mat at x 700, y 250, 420 by 260, with room for two cards and their two objects side by side and the two bottom numbers lighting amber above it together, and a Like button and an Unlike button under it, each labelled in words. On the fourth phase two identical objects, two chocolate bars 620 long and 100 tall from one common left edge at x 160, y 250 and y 370, or two jugs from one common base, with their equal parts drawn in, stand one above the other, and under them a line-up row of three or four objects with a slot for each place at y 520, smallest first. The object that is tapped as the bigger one gets a vermilion ring and is labelled Bigger. A Check button sits under the bins and the mat, labelled in words, and a Shape view button beside it swaps every real object for a plain strip cut into the same equal parts. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a fraction bar key, for typing a fraction into the answer slot, and the Like and Unlike buttons on the third phase. A card whose bottom number is above ten, such as a sixteenth, is drawn with no picture and is sorted by its two numbers alone. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object, never by tinting it. The parts a fraction counts, the ones coloured or taken, sit on a deep blue plate, in a deep blue basket or inside a deep blue ring, labelled Coloured or Taken, and a plain drawn part that is coloured is deep blue. The other parts of the same whole, the ones left, sit on an amber plate or in an amber basket, labelled Left. A whole shown entire sits inside a green outline, labelled Whole, and a bracket spanning one whole is green. The bigger of two like fractions gets a vermilion ring, labelled Bigger. A part of a plain drawn shape that is not coloured stays warm white inside its near-black outline, every cut line is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last row of objects stands from the smallest to the biggest, the biggest ringed in vermilion, with each card's fraction written under its object.

phases.win: the unit cards sit in their bin, each object showing a single part on its blue plate
phases.does: reads the top number of each card, drags it to a bin, then taps Check
phases.goal: a fraction with one as its top number is a unit fraction
phases.says: Look at the top number on each card. Which cards have a one on top?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a pizza card has a one on top and a bigger number below. Is it a unit fraction? How many slices are taken?
phases.feels: the cards with one slice, square or mark taken gathering in one bin, however big the pizza or bar was
phases.hands: Draw a pizza, a chocolate bar and a jug on paper, cut each into equal parts, and write the fraction on the back. Sort them into two piles, the ones with one part taken and the rest.
phases.tries: First rung: point to the top number of the card. Second rung: count the slices on the blue plate beside the pizza. Third rung: the same task with only two cards on the tray, before the full tray returns.

wrong.why: the bottom number is the big, easy one to read first
wrong.move: puts a card in the Top number is one bin because of its bottom number
wrong.screen: the object's parts on the blue plate are counted: the taken slices light amber in turn, and the count is written beside the top number

wrong.why: a pizza with many slices looks like a lot of fraction
wrong.move: leaves a card with one slice taken out of the bin, because the pizza has many slices
wrong.screen: the pizza's other slices dim to half strength, so the single slice on the blue plate stands alone beside the one on top

phases.screen: a tray of six cards, each with its pizza, bar, jug, cake, laddoos or kites, and two empty bins, Top number is one and Not one
phases.soWhat: a unit fraction has one as its top number
phases.concept: Unit fractions: the top number is one

phases.win: an improper card shows one whole pizza on the blue plate and more slices from a second pizza
phases.does: reads both numbers of a card, drags it to a bin, and watches the pizzas and bars
phases.goal: a fraction is proper when its top is smaller than its bottom, and improper when it is bigger or the same
phases.says: Is the top number smaller than the bottom number? Look at the pictures too.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a cake card has a smaller number on top than on the bottom. Is it more than one whole cake, or less?
phases.feels: a second pizza sliding in beside a card exactly when its top number gets past the bottom
phases.hands: Use paper pizzas cut into equal slices. Put more slices on a plate than one pizza holds, cut a second paper pizza, and say whether the top number or the bottom number is bigger.
phases.tries: First rung: read the top number, then the bottom number. Second rung: look at whether the first pizza is full. Third rung: the same task with a card whose top number is only one more than its bottom number.

wrong.why: a big number feels like a lot, and a lot feels like more than one
wrong.move: calls a card proper because its top number is a big number
wrong.screen: the two numbers are set side by side and the slices on the plate are counted, and a second pizza slides in only where the first pizza is full

wrong.why: it is only one pizza, so it does not look like more than one whole
wrong.move: calls a card with the same number top and bottom proper
wrong.screen: the whole pizza is ringed in green and labelled Whole, with the words top number the same as bottom number beside it

phases.screen: a tray of cards and two bins, Proper and Improper, with a second pizza, bar or cake beside any card that needs one
phases.soWhat: a proper fraction has a top number smaller than its bottom number, and an improper fraction has a top number bigger than or the same as its bottom number
phases.concept: Proper and improper: is the top number smaller?

phases.win: the two bottom numbers light together, the two objects show parts of one size, and the mat reads Like
phases.does: puts two cards on the mat, reads the lit bottom numbers, and taps Like or Unlike
phases.goal: fractions with the same bottom number are like, and fractions with different bottom numbers are unlike
phases.says: Put two cards on the mat. Do the two bottom numbers match?
phases.check: Away from the screen: two jug cards have different top numbers and the same bottom number. Are they like or unlike?
phases.feels: the two bottom numbers lighting up together on the mat, and the top numbers staying quiet
phases.hands: Write six fractions on cards, each beside a drawn pizza or bar. Lay two on the desk and cover their top numbers with a finger, so only the bottom numbers can be read. Say like or unlike.
phases.tries: First rung: cover the top numbers. Second rung: say the two bottom numbers aloud. Third rung: the same task with a pair whose bottom numbers are one apart.

wrong.why: the matching numbers are the first thing the eye catches
wrong.move: says like because the two top numbers are the same
wrong.screen: the two bottom numbers light amber together and the top numbers dim to half strength, and the two objects show parts of different sizes

wrong.why: different amounts taken feel like different fractions
wrong.move: says unlike because the two cards show different amounts taken
wrong.screen: the two objects are shown cut into the same number of equal parts, with the bottom number lit on both, and the words same bottom number appear beside them

phases.screen: a mat with room for two cards and their two objects, and a pair of cards waiting beside it
phases.soWhat: fractions with the same bottom number are like fractions, and fractions with different bottom numbers are unlike
phases.concept: Like and unlike: do the bottom numbers match?

phases.win: the bigger one gets a vermilion ring and is labelled Bigger
phases.does: taps the object with more parts taken, then drags objects into a row from the smallest to the biggest
phases.goal: between two like fractions the one with the bigger top number is bigger
phases.says: The parts are the same size. Which one has more parts taken?
phases.check: Away from the screen: two like jug cards have top numbers three and five. Which jug has more juice, and how do you know?
phases.feels: the longer taken stretch getting its vermilion ring, with all the parts the same size
phases.hands: Draw chocolate bars of ten squares, eat a different number of squares on each, and line them up from one left edge. Say which bar has the most eaten and write each fraction.
phases.tries: First rung: check that the two objects have the same number of equal parts. Second rung: count the parts taken from each. Third rung: the same task with the taken parts counted aloud while they light up in turn.

wrong.why: the bottom number is the big number on the card, so it feels like the one that counts
wrong.move: says the bar with the bigger bottom number is bigger, when the bottom numbers match
wrong.screen: both bottom numbers light amber as the same number, and the squares are counted by the ones taken, the longer taken stretch glowing

wrong.why: two fractions on one screen look as if they can always be compared
wrong.move: tries to compare two cards that have different bottom numbers
wrong.screen: the mat says in words that fractions with different bottom numbers need more steps that are not met yet, and offers a pair of like cards

wrong.why: the biggest one catches the eye and goes first
wrong.move: lines the objects up from the biggest
wrong.screen: the first slot is marked Smallest in words, and the object placed there is checked against the object beside it

phases.screen: two identical objects cut into equal parts, side by side from one common edge, and a line-up row
phases.soWhat: between two like fractions, the one with the bigger top number is bigger

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the line-up row is finished in the right order, the chocolate bars slide together into one staircase, each step one square longer than the one before, and the biggest gets its vermilion ring. On any jug card, the juice rises one mark at a time to the top number as the card is picked up.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing sorted yet. On the first phase the tray holds six cards, each with its pizza, chocolate bar, jug, cake, plate of laddoos or row of kites, and the two bins Top number is one and Not one stand empty at the right. On the second the bins are Proper and Improper, and the improper cards already have their second pizza, bar or cake beside the first. On the third the mat is empty and a pair of cards waits beside it. On the fourth two identical objects stand side by side from one common edge. One thing moves, once: the first card, or the first object on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any cards sorted into any bins, any two cards on the mat, two identical objects stood from one edge and a row of objects lined up. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, each with a pizza, a chocolate bar, a jug, a cake, laddoos or kites: unit cards, proper and improper cards, like and unlike pairs, and the bigger of two like fractions.
voiceLines: Some fraction cards, and a real thing beside each one.
Look at the top number on each card. Which cards have a one on top?
Is the top number smaller than the bottom number? Look at the pictures too.
Put two cards on the mat. Do the two bottom numbers match?
The parts are the same size. Which one has more parts taken?
A new set of cards. Read the numbers before you drop one.
Free play. Sort, match and line up the pizzas and bars as you like.
Look at the picture again. Count the parts on the plate, then all the parts.
You told the kinds apart by reading the top and bottom numbers.

observations.why: the top number counts the parts taken, and a unit fraction has exactly one of them.
observations.soWhat: a unit fraction has one as its top number.
observations.observe: A card with a one on top showed a single slice, square or mark on the blue plate, however many parts the pizza or bar had.

observations.why: one pizza holds only as many slices as its bottom number, so more slices on the plate need a second pizza.
observations.soWhat: an improper fraction is one whole or more, and its top number is bigger than or the same as its bottom number.
observations.observe: A card whose top number was bigger than its bottom number slid a second pizza in beside the first.

observations.why: like and unlike are about the size of the parts, which the bottom number gives, and not about how many are taken.
observations.soWhat: fractions with the same bottom number are like, whatever their top numbers are.
observations.observe: The mat lit the two bottom numbers together, and the top numbers stayed dark.

observations.why: the two bars were cut into the same number of equal squares, so more squares taken is a longer taken stretch.
observations.soWhat: between two like fractions, the one with the bigger top number is bigger.
observations.observe: The chocolate bar with more squares taken reached further from the left edge, and the squares were all the same size.

serves.exercise: writing the fraction of the matches won and naming its type
circling the unit fractions in a list of sixteen
circling the proper fractions and ticking the improper fractions in a list of sixteen

source_tool.description: A tray of fraction cards sits at the left of the working area. Each card shows a fraction written with its top number above a level line above its bottom number, and beside it a real object drawn in its own natural colours and cut into as many equal parts as the bottom number says: a pizza cut into slices, a chocolate bar with its squares, a jug of juice with equal marks, a plate of laddoos, a row of kites or a round cake. The parts the top number counts sit on a small deep blue plate beside the object, or inside a deep blue ring on a jug, and the parts left stay on the object. Two labelled bins stand at the right. On the first phase they are Top number is one and Not one. On the second they are Proper and Improper, and a card whose top number is bigger than its bottom number slides a second pizza, bar or cake in beside the first, so one whole and more is drawn; a card with the same number top and bottom shows exactly one whole object inside a green outline. Dragging a card into a bin drops it there, and the Check button reads the whole sort back against the pictures without marking or clearing anything. On the third phase a mat takes two cards at a time, shows their two objects cut as they are, lights the two bottom numbers together, and the child taps Like or Unlike. The mat never compares the two: if a child asks, it says in words that fractions with different bottom numbers need more steps that are not met yet. On the fourth phase two identical objects, two chocolate bars of one size or two jugs with the same equal marks, stand from one common edge. The child taps the one with more parts taken, and it gets a vermilion ring labelled Bigger. Then three or four like objects, paper strips of ten squares among them, are dragged into a row from the smallest to the biggest. A Shape view button swaps each real object for a plain strip. A number pad types a fraction. A card whose bottom number is above ten, such as a sixteenth, is drawn with no picture and is sorted by its two numbers alone, because an object is drawn only up to tenths. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many cards have been sorted.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a round chapati with its toasted spots, a pizza with toppings, a cake, a chocolate bar with its squares, a jug of juice with equal marks, laddoos, mangoes, bananas, kites, balloons, pencils, marbles, bangles, books. The object is the thing the child works on, and a plain shape appears only as a second view the child can switch to.
A part is never drawn without its whole. The whole object stays in the frame, entire, with the parts that were not taken still drawn and still countable.

Every division into parts is made by a drawn cut line, score line or gap, never by a change of colour alone, and the cuts go in before anything is taken, so the bottom number can be counted whether anything is taken or not.

Where a fraction says its parts are equal, every part is drawn the same size and the same shape. Where a stage deliberately shows unequal parts, such as a roti torn unevenly, it says so in its own label and no fraction name is written against them.

Taking a part is something the child does: a slice is lifted onto the deep blue plate, a mango is dropped into the deep blue basket. The plate and the basket carry the colour code, and the object keeps its own colours.
A fraction is always written with its top number above a level line and its bottom number below it, both upright and centred. The line is never slanted and the two numbers are never set side by side.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
Two like fractions are shown as two objects of the same size laid one under the other from one common left edge, so that the taken parts ending in different places carries the claim.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a part, a counter or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a chapati stays toasted brown and a mango stays yellow. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object, never by tinting the object. The parts a fraction counts, the ones coloured or taken, sit on a deep blue plate, in a deep blue basket or inside a deep blue ring, and a plain drawn part that is coloured is deep blue. The other parts of that same whole, the ones left, sit on an amber plate or in an amber basket. A whole shown entire sits inside a green outline, and a bracket spanning one whole is green. The bigger of two like fractions gets a vermilion ring. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every cut line, outline and plain edge is near-black, and a part of a drawn shape that is not coloured stays warm white inside its outline. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Coloured or Taken, Left, Whole and Bigger, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the picture again. Count the parts on the plate, then all the parts.
voice.onNext: A new set of cards. Read the numbers before you drop one.
voice.opening: Some fraction cards, and a real thing beside each one.
voice.onFinish: You told the kinds apart by reading the top and bottom numbers.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Sort, match and line up the pizzas and bars as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Unit fractions: the top number is one
Proper and improper: is the top number smaller?
Like and unlike: do the bottom numbers match?

placement.where: After the class has coloured paper strips of ten squares, lined them up and said which reaches further, and has cut a paper pizza or a drawn chocolate bar into equal parts. The tool is what turns a card into a real object at once, slides a second pizza in for an improper card, and stands two identical objects from one edge, which a printed list cannot do.

answer_key.rule: A unit fraction has one as its top number. A proper fraction has a top number smaller than its bottom number, so it is less than one whole pizza, bar or cake. An improper fraction has a top number bigger than its bottom number, or the same, so it is one whole or more. Like fractions have the same bottom number, and unlike fractions have different bottom numbers, whatever the top numbers are. Between two like fractions the one with the bigger top number is bigger, because the parts are the same size and there are more of them. Fractions with different bottom numbers are not compared here.
answer_key.wrong: The card is shown again with its object beside its written fraction, the top number and the parts on the blue plate are counted together, then the bottom number and all the parts of the object. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Look at the top number of each card, not the bottom number.
The pizza card 1/5 has a one on top, and the chocolate bar card 2/5 has a two on top.
The jug card 1/9 has a one on top, and the cake card 6/9 has a six on top.
A fraction with a one on top is a unit fraction. So the pizza card and the jug card go in the bin.
items.answer: The pizza card 1/5 and the jug card 1/9
items.question: The tray holds a pizza card 1/5, a chocolate bar card 2/5, a jug card 1/9 and a cake card 6/9. Which cards go in the bin Top number is one?
items.checkpoint: A unit fraction has one on top.
items.misconception: Looks at the bottom number, so the chocolate bar card 2/5 goes in the bin with the pizza card 1/5 because both are fifths.

steps: The bottom number is 4, so each pizza is cut into 4 equal slices.
Put 7 slices on the blue plate. One pizza holds only 4, so a second pizza slides in.
One whole pizza and 3 more slices are on the plate, so the fraction is more than one whole.
The top number 7 is bigger than the bottom number 4, so 7/4 is improper.
items.question: A pizza card shows 7/4, and every pizza is cut into 4 slices. Is 7/4 proper or improper? Use the pizzas to see.
items.checkpoint: An improper fraction has a top number bigger than, or the same as, its bottom number.
items.misconception: Calls it proper because it looks like any other fraction, without comparing the top and bottom numbers.

steps: The mat lights the two bottom numbers, 5 and 9.
The pizza is cut into 5 slices and the chocolate bar into 9 squares, so the parts are different sizes.
5 and 9 are different numbers, so the bottom numbers do not match. Fractions with different bottom numbers are unlike fractions.
The top numbers do not matter for like and unlike. Only the bottom numbers do.
items.question: The mat holds a pizza card 4/5 and a chocolate bar card 4/9. Are the two cards like or unlike?
items.checkpoint: Like fractions have the same bottom number.
items.misconception: Says like because both top numbers are 4 and four parts are on the blue plate in each picture.

steps: Both bars have ten squares, so every square is the same size.
One bar has 6 squares eaten, so it shows 6/10. The other shows 9/10.
9 is bigger than 6, so the eaten squares of the 9 bar reach further from the left edge.
items.question: Two chocolate bars of the same size each have ten squares. One has 6 squares eaten and the other has 9. Which fraction is bigger?
items.checkpoint: With the same bottom number, the bigger top number is the bigger fraction.
items.misconception: Looks at the bottom numbers, which match, and then cannot choose, instead of comparing the top numbers.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A chocolate bar has 10 equal squares and 1 square is eaten. The card says 1/10. Is it a unit fraction? How do you know?
items.final_answer: Yes, because the top number is one

items.question: A round cake is cut into 9 equal slices and 8 slices are eaten. The card says 8/9. Is it proper or improper?
items.final_answer: Proper, because 8 is smaller than 9, so it is less than one whole cake

items.question: Two plates each hold 9 laddoos. On one plate 1 laddoo is taken and on the other plate 7 are taken. The cards say 1/9 and 7/9. Are they like or unlike?
items.final_answer: Like, because both bottom numbers are 9

items.question: Two jugs are the same size, and each is marked in 9 equal marks. One is filled with juice to 7 marks and the other to 4 marks. Which jug has more juice?
items.final_answer: The jug filled to 7/9, because the bottom numbers match and 7 is bigger than 4

items.question: The tray holds a pizza card 1/3, a kite row card 1/7, a cake card 2/9 and a jug card 1/10. Which card is not a unit fraction?
items.final_answer: The cake card 2/9, because its top number is two and not one

items.question: The tray holds a pizza card 9/5, a chocolate bar card 5/8, a cake card 8/8 and a jug card 2/9. Which cards are improper?
items.final_answer: The pizza card 9/5 and the cake card 8/8, because their top numbers are bigger than or the same as their bottom numbers

items.question: Four cards wait on the tray: a laddoo plate 2/9, a pizza 5/9, a chocolate bar 4/9 and a kite row 4/7. Which card is the odd one out?
items.final_answer: The kite row 4/7, because the other three have 9 as the bottom number, so they are like fractions

items.question: A child puts a pizza card 3/7 and a chocolate bar card 3/10 on the mat and asks which one is bigger. What does the mat say?
items.final_answer: The bottom numbers are different, so these are unlike fractions. Sort and Compare only compares like fractions. This needs more steps that are not met yet

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: moves a fraction card from the tray into a bin or onto the mat
reads the sort back against the objects without marking or clearing it
say whether the two cards on the mat have matching bottom numbers
picks the one with more parts taken, which gets a vermilion ring and reads Bigger
swaps each real object for a plain strip cut into the same equal parts, and back
types a fraction, with a bar key between the top and bottom numbers

teaching_notes: Cut a paper pizza and draw a chocolate bar of ten squares before the tool opens, and colour paper strips of ten squares and line them up from the fewest squares coloured to the most. Ask the child to read the top number and the bottom number of every card aloud before it is dropped in a bin. Wait for them to say which number they looked at. For improper cards ask how many pizzas it takes to hold all the slices. For like and unlike, cover the top numbers with a finger, so only the bottom numbers can be read. On the last phase say the rule in the child's words: the parts are the same size, so more parts taken is bigger. Do not compare two fractions with different bottom numbers, even when the child can guess; say that it needs more steps and has not been learned yet.
generation_prompt: Build a fraction sorting tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A tray of fraction cards sits at the left of the working area. Each card shows a fraction with its top number above a level line above its bottom number, beside a real everyday object drawn as a hand-built SVG illustration in its own natural colours and cut into as many equal parts as the bottom number says: a pizza with toppings, a chocolate bar with its squares, a jug of juice with equal marks, a plate of laddoos, a row of kites or a round cake. The parts the top number counts sit on a small deep blue plate beside the object, or inside a deep blue ring on a jug. Two labelled bins stand at the right: Top number is one and Not one on the first phase, Proper and Improper on the second. An improper card slides a second pizza, bar or cake in beside the first, so one whole and more is drawn, and a card with equal top and bottom shows one whole object in a green outline. Dragging drops a card into a bin, and a Check button reads the sort back without marking or clearing it. On the third phase a mat takes two cards and their two objects and lights the two bottom numbers, with Like and Unlike buttons, and it never compares the two. On the fourth phase two identical objects stand from one common edge, tapping the one with more parts taken puts a vermilion ring on it and labels it Bigger, and three or four like objects are dragged into a row from the smallest to the biggest. A Shape view button swaps each object for a plain strip. A number pad types a fraction. A card whose bottom number is above ten has no picture and is sorted by its two numbers alone. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of cards sorted. No photographs, no people and no faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read the top number and the bottom number of each card. Look at the pizza, bar or jug. Drop the card in its bin. Then line up like things from the smallest to the biggest.
